title: Northern gannet diet revealed by combining bird-borne camera, faecal DNA, and regurgitate data from a focal colony with a multi-colony literature review
content:
Abstract
Quantifying marine predator diets is an essential means for understanding the drivers of changing behaviour and demography but requires knowledge of spatio-temporal and methodological variability to establish effective baselines. Here, we characterize the diet of the North Atlantic’s largest seabird—northern gannets Morus bassanus—by conducting a dietary deep-dive from a single large UK colony (Grassholm) using multiple techniques across several years combined with a review of diet literature from across their breeding range. Based on 14 years of spontaneous regurgitates (n = 656; 2006–2025), 3 years of bird-borne video footage (n = 103; 2016–2019) and a single year of high throughput DNA sequences in faeces (n = 33; 2024) we found that Grassholm gannet diets were dominated by three functional groups (i) forage fish (sandeel Ammodytes spp., sprat Sprattus sprattus, sardine Sardina pilchardus), (ii) large pelagic fish (Atlantic mackerel Scomber scombrus, herring Clupea harengus, garfish Belone belone) and (iii) demersal fish scavenged/depredated from fishing vessels (e.g. haddock Melanogrammus aeglefinus, red gurnard Chelidonichthys cuculus and flatfish—confirmed from video). Long-term regurgitate data suggest inter-annual variability—especially for demersal and large pelagic fish—but with no clear temporal trends. By comparison, videos suggested a relatively higher incidence of forage fish, but not in all years. Dietary DNA from a single year indicated ~70% forage fish compared with ~30% from video and ~12% from regurgitates suggesting methodological biases. A review of gannet regurgitates from across their breeding range (13 colonies, n = 14 351 samples, spanning 1973–2017) revealed a similar diversity of fish diet. Large pelagic fish were generally the most consistent food with forage fish and demersal fish being more spatially and temporally variable. Our study reaffirms that gannets are eclectic piscivores but quantifying their dietary diversity accurately requires information from a range of methodological approaches, locations, and over time. The continued success of gannets may be predicated on this broad niche but changes in offshore development, fisheries, and the impact of avian influenza provide challenges ahead.
